To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the rate of reduction in viable bacteria is dependent upon the antibiotic concentration and the time the bacteria are exposed to that concentration.

the area under concentration curve (AUC) might be of importance for antimicrobial activity rather than the initial antibiotic concentration, and that the inclusion of pharmacokinetics in antimicrobial susceptibility test might add a new dimensions to the understanding of the activity of antibiotics.
the in vitro model of fluctuating antibiotic concentrations is a good tool for the evaluation of the in vitro activity of antimicrobials.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the kinetics and the regrowth of bacteria in the presence of fluctuating concentrations of antimicrobials.
the development of a new method to determine the antimicrobial activity in vitro of substances which are not readily amenable to the standard agar diffusion method.
the development of mathematical models to describe antibiotic kinetics in vitro and in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the in vitro model used in this study was able to mimic the in vivo situation with respect to the kill kinetics of bacteria exposed to fluctuating antibiotic concentrations, and the regrowth pattern after exposure to these concentrations.
the in vitro pharmacokinetic model provides a useful tool to investigate antimicrobial activity under fluctuating antibiotic concentrations.
in vivo pharmacokinetics are of great importance in antimicrobial therapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the in vitro pharmacodynamic model can predict the outcome of in vivo antibiotic therapy.
the area under concentration curve is more important than the peak concentration in the determination of antimicrobial activity.
the area under concentration curve might be a better measure of the antimicrobial activity than the initial concentration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to consider the pharmacokinetic profile of an antimicrobial substance when determining susceptibility testing.
we should be careful when interpreting MIC values, as these are only a snapshot of a very complex interaction between bacteria and antibiotics.
in vitro antimicrobial susceptibility testing may be more predictive of clinical outcome than is generally appreciated.
